text: Accordingly I went to one who had the reputation of wisdom, and observed him--his name I need not mention; he was a politician whom I selected for examination--and the result was as follows: When I began to talk with him, I could not help thinking that he was not really wise, although he was thought wise by many, and still wiser by himself; and thereupon I tried to explain to him that he thought himself wise, but was not really wise; and the consequence was that he hated me, and his enmity was shared by several who were present and heard me. So I left him, saying to myself, as I went away: Well, although I do not suppose that either of us knows anything really beautiful and good, I am better off than he is,--for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know. In this latter particular, then, I seem to have slightly the advantage of him.
note: Humility: knowing that you do not know

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
keywords: knowing that I do not know
tags.when_helps: Someone around confident experts, or overconfident themselves, reflecting on admitting what they don't know.

core_idea: Wisdom begins with knowing you don't know

text: Some one will say: And are you not ashamed, Socrates, of a course of life which is likely to bring you to an untimely end? To him I may fairly answer: There you are mistaken: a man who is good for anything ought not to calculate the chance of living or dying; he ought only to consider whether in doing anything he is doing right or wrong--acting the part of a good man or of a bad.
note: Doing right matters more than fear of death

keywords: right or wrong, not living or dying
tags.when_helps: Someone tempted to compromise their principles out of fear for their safety or position.

core_idea: Ask only whether you act rightly

text: For the fear of death is indeed the pretence of wisdom, and not real wisdom, being a pretence of knowing the unknown; and no one knows whether death, which men in their fear apprehend to be the greatest evil, may not be the greatest good. Is not this ignorance of a disgraceful sort, the ignorance which is the conceit that a man knows what he does not know?
note: Fear of death; we do not know what death is

keywords: fear of death as false wisdom
tags.safety_reason: Suggests death may be the greatest good, which a reader in distress could take as encouragement to welcome it.
tags.when_helps: Someone who fears death philosophically and wants to question whether that fear is justified.

plain: Fearing death is pretending to know what we don't. No one knows whether death, which people dread as the worst evil, might be the greatest good. Thinking you know what you don't is shameful ignorance.
core_idea: Fearing death claims knowledge we lack

text: For I do nothing but go about persuading you all, old and young alike, not to take thought for your persons or your properties, but first and chiefly to care about the greatest improvement of the soul. I tell you that virtue is not given by money, but that from virtue comes money and every other good of man, public as well as private.
note: Caring for the soul before money and status

tags.when_helps: Someone absorbed by money and appearance who wants to put the growth of character first.

core_idea: Care for your soul before body or wealth

text: Some one will say: Yes, Socrates, but cannot you hold your tongue, and then you may go into a foreign city, and no one will interfere with you? Now I have great difficulty in making you understand my answer to this. For if I tell you that to do as you say would be a disobedience to the God, and therefore that I cannot hold my tongue, you will not believe that I am serious; and if I say again that daily to discourse about virtue, and of those other things about which you hear me examining myself and others, is the greatest good of man, and that the unexamined life is not worth living, you are still less likely to believe me. Yet I say what is true, although a thing of which it is hard for me to persuade you.
note: Purpose and self-examination; the unexamined life

tags.when_helps: Someone pressured to keep quiet about what they believe, weighing silence against a life of honest inquiry.

core_idea: The unexamined life is not worth living

text: The difficulty, my friends, is not to avoid death, but to avoid unrighteousness; for that runs faster than death.

tags.when_helps: Someone tempted to do wrong to escape danger, reminded that wrongdoing is the greater threat.

core_idea: Avoiding wrongdoing is harder than avoiding death

text: If you think that by killing men you can prevent some one from censuring your evil lives, you are mistaken; that is not a way of escape which is either possible or honourable; the easiest and the noblest way is not to be disabling others, but to be improving yourselves.
note: facing criticism by self-improvement, not silencing critics

tags.when_helps: Someone tempted to silence their critics, or being silenced, who needs to hear that self-improvement is the answer.

core_idea: Improve yourself rather than silence critics

text: Now if you suppose that there is no consciousness, but a sleep like the sleep of him who is undisturbed even by dreams, death will be an unspeakable gain. For if a person were to select the night in which his sleep was undisturbed even by dreams, and were to compare with this the other days and nights of his life, and then were to tell us how many days and nights he had passed in the course of his life better and more pleasantly than this one, I think that any man, I will not say a private man, but even the great king will not find many such days or nights, when compared with the others. Now if death be of such a nature, I say that to die is gain; for eternity is then only a single night.
note: fear of death; death as peaceful sleep

tags.safety_reason: Calls death an unspeakable gain and better than most days of life, which presents dying as desirable to a distressed reader.
tags.when_helps: Someone facing terminal illness who wants a calm, reasoned argument that death need not be feared.

text: Wherefore, O judges, be of good cheer about death, and know of a certainty, that no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.
note: comfort facing death; goodness cannot be harmed

keywords: no evil to a good man
tags.when_helps: Someone afraid of death or harm who draws courage from the belief that goodness cannot be truly harmed.

core_idea: No evil can befall a good person

text: The hour of departure has arrived, and we go our ways--I to die, and you to live. Which is better God only knows.
note: parting, mortality, humility about what is better

tags.safety_reason: Leaves open that dying may be better than living, which a distressed reader could read as death being preferable.
tags.when_helps: Someone at a parting near the end of life, accepting that no one knows which path is better.
